OPEN
This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
Let $f$ be a random completely multiplicative function, where for each prime $p$ we independently choose $f(p)\in \{-1,1\}$ uniformly at random. Is it true that\[\limsup_{N\to \infty}\frac{\sum_{m\leq N}f(m)}{\sqrt{N}}=\infty\]with probability $1$?
#1144: [Va99,1.11]
number theory | 
probability
This model of a random multiplicative function is sometimes called a Rademacher function, although this is sometimes reserved for a merely multiplicative function (which is $0$ on non-squarefree integers). See [520] for the partial sums of this alternative model.
It should also be compared to another popular model of random completely multiplicative functions, Steinhaus functions, which have $f(p)$ uniformly distributed over the unit circle.
Atherfold [At25] has proved that, almost surely,\[\sum_{m\leq N}f(m)\ll N^{1/2}(\log N)^{1+o(1)}.\]
Additional thanks to: Adam Harper

A full proof 
claimed by Sigurd William Rachlew Høystad (using GPT 6 Astra, GPT 5.6 Sol Pro, Fable 5).
 Summary:
 For a completely multiplicative random function with independent fair signs at primes, the normalized partial sums have almost surely infinite positive limsup. The proof transfers squarefree Gaussian lower bounds to the complete model using stationary covariance comparisons and uniform error estimates, then applies fresh-prime Gaussian approximation.
 Notes:
 The standalone Lean build and final theorem’s axiom audit passed. The theorem depends only on Lean’s standard axioms.
